results.prompt: Compare the tiers and tell me the best value.
Show the costs and explain the largest one.
results.raw:
No cost data was shared in this conversation, so the numbers below are an illustrative breakdown of a typical monthly infrastructure/software bill. Swap in your real figures and the structure still holds.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([m1, ch1, tbl1])
m1 = Metric("Total monthly cost", "35 000 kr", "Illustrative breakdown, not your actuals")
ch1 = Chart("bar", "Cost by category (kr/month)", ["Compute", "Licenses & SaaS", "Storage & backup", "Bandwidth", "Support & monitoring"], [{name: "Cost (kr)", values: [18400, 6800, 4200, 3100, 2500]}])
tbl1 = Table("Breakdown", ["Category", "Monthly", "Share", "Driver"], [["Compute (VMs/K8s)", "18 400 kr", "53%", "Always-on capacity, request over-provisioning"], ["Licenses & SaaS", "6 800 kr", "19%", "Per-seat tooling, mostly flat regardless of usage"], ["Storage & backup", "4 200 kr", "12%", "Snapshot retention keeps growing"], ["Bandwidth / egress", "3 100 kr", "9%", "Cross-region and egress traffic"], ["Support & monitoring", "2 500 kr", "7%", "Observability stack and vendor support"]])
:::

**The largest cost is Compute at 18 400 kr/month — about 53% of the total**, and it is more than twice the next largest line.

Why it dominates:

- **It is a capacity cost, not a usage cost.** You pay for provisioned nodes whether or not they are busy. Licenses and support are per-seat and roughly flat; compute scales with how much you keep switched on.
- **Over-provisioning compounds it.** If CPU requests are set to 2× actual usage, the scheduler reserves roughly double the nodes needed — the most common single source of waste in this category.
- **Non-production environments rarely sleep.** Staging and dev clusters running 24/7 can easily be 20–30% of compute spend while serving almost no traffic.
- **Restarts and retries hide here too.** Churn from failing pods or aggressive autoscaling cycles quietly adds node-hours.

Practical levers, roughly in order of payoff: right-size CPU/memory requests against real p95 usage, run non-prod on a schedule (nights and weekends off), then apply committed-use or spot pricing to the steady-state baseline. Together these typically cut compute 25–40%, which moves the total far more than optimising any other line.

results.prompt: Chart the growth and interpret it.
results.raw:
I don't have a dataset attached, so here's an illustrative growth curve (indexed to 100 at the start of the period) — the point is to show what the shape says, not to invent your numbers. Give me your actual figures and I'll re-chart them exactly.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([g1, c1, c2])
g1 = Grid([m1, m2, m3])
m1 = Metric("Avg. quarterly growth", "23.1%", "Compounding, over 8 quarters")
m2 = Metric("Implied annual growth", "2.3x", "At a steady 23% per quarter")
m3 = Metric("Doubling time", "~3.3 quarters", "Roughly 10 months")
c1 = Card("Growth path — indexed, illustrative", [ch1])
ch1 = Chart("line", "", ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4", "Q5", "Q6", "Q7", "Q8"], [{name:"Index (start = 100)", values:[100, 124, 152, 187, 231, 284, 349, 430]}])
c2 = Card("Quarter-over-quarter growth rate", [ch2])
ch2 = Chart("bar", "", ["Q2", "Q3", "Q4", "Q5", "Q6", "Q7", "Q8"], [{name:"QoQ growth %", values:[24, 22.6, 23, 23.5, 22.9, 22.9, 23.2]}])
:::

**How to read it**

- **The curve bends upward, but the growth rate is flat.** That combination is the signature of *compounding*: each quarter grows by roughly the same percentage of a bigger base. The acceleration you see is arithmetic, not a breakout.
- **Stable, not spiking.** The second chart stays in a 22.6–24% band. There's no single quarter carrying the period — which is good news for planning, because it means the trend is a process you can model, not a one-off event.
- **The practical unit is the doubling time, not the slope.** At ~23% per quarter, you double roughly every 3–4 quarters; a rate that looks modest per quarter is 2.3× per year. That's also why small rate changes compound hard: 23% vs 18% is the difference between doubling in ~10 months and ~13.
- **What would change the conclusion:** if the *rate* line starts sliding while the curve still rises, you've moved from compounding to a decline disguised as growth. If the rate rises too, you can't extrapolate the same doubling time — you'd be looking at a regime change, not a trend.

Tell me the metric, period length and actual values, and whether you want the y-axis linear or log (log makes a constant percentage rate look like a straight line — the fastest way to spot a rate that's quietly decaying).

results.prompt: Which is better, React or Vue? Compare.
results.raw:
"Better" depends on what you're optimizing for — here's the honest breakdown.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([cmp, d1, tbl])
cmp = Comparison("React vs Vue", [r1, v1])
r1 = {name:"React", attributes:["Huge ecosystem & job market","JSX — JavaScript-first templating","Flexible, unopinionated; you pick the rest","Best for large/enterprise apps, React Native","Steeper learning curve (hooks, memoization)"]}
v1 = {name:"Vue", attributes:["Gentler learning curve","SFCs with <template>, <script>, <style>","Opinionated defaults, batteries included","Great for small/medium apps, progressive adoption","Smaller talent pool & ecosystem"]}
d1 = Divider()
tbl = Table("By dimension", ["Dimension","React","Vue"], [["Learning curve","Steeper","Gentle"],["Templating","JSX","HTML templates"],["Flexibility","Very high","Balanced/opinionated"],["Ecosystem size","Largest","Good, smaller"],["Job market","Broadest","Niche but real"],["Mobile","React Native","Capacitor/Ionic"],["Performance","Excellent","Excellent"],["Best for","Large teams, complex apps","Fast delivery, smaller teams"]])
:::

**The short answer:** neither is objectively better — they're both excellent, and both will comfortably build anything you're likely to build.

- **Choose React** if you want maximum hiring pool and ecosystem, are building something large or long-lived, need React Native, or are targeting enterprise work.
- **Choose Vue** if you want to ship faster with less ceremony, are a solo dev or small team, or value a single-file component model that reads closer to plain HTML.

The pragmatic tiebreaker most teams use: **pick the one your team already knows.** Switching costs outweigh the technical differences here.

root = Form("Contact us", [f1, f2, f3, f4, f5, row1])

f1 = Field("Name", [i1], "So we know who we're replying to")
i1 = Input("Your full name", $name, "Jane Doe")

f2 = Field("Email", [i2], "We never share your address")
i2 = Input("you@example.com", $email, "you@example.com")

f3 = Field("Topic", [s1])
s1 = Select("What is this about?", $topic, ["General question", "Sales", "Support", "Bug report", "Partnership"])

f4 = Field("Message", [t1], "The more detail, the faster we can help")
t1 = Textarea("How can we help?", $message, "Tell us a bit about it...")

f5 = Field("Priority", [sw1])
sw1 = Switch("This is urgent", $urgent)

row1 = Row([b1, b2])
b1 = Button("Send message", "conversation.create", {content: "Contact form submission"})
b2 = Button("Clear form", @Reset($name))
:::

A few notes on how it's built: **Topic** uses a dropdown since the options are mutually exclusive, **Priority** is a switch so it's a single yes/no, and the email field carries helper text rather than inline validation so the form stays uncluttered. The Clear button resets the name field — if you'd like, I can wire up a full reset across all fields or add a phone number / file attachment field.

results.prompt: Create a survey form with a rating.
results.raw:
Here's a ready-to-use survey with several rating inputs and a live score that updates as the form is filled in.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([f1, c1])
f1 = Form("Customer satisfaction survey", [fld1, fld2, fld3, fld4, fld5, fld6, btn1])
fld1 = Field("Your name", [in1], "Optional, but helps us follow up")
in1 = Input("Name", $name)
fld2 = Field("Overall satisfaction", [r1], "Pick the option that fits best")
r1 = Radio("How satisfied are you overall?", $overall, ["Very satisfied", "Satisfied", "Neutral", "Dissatisfied"])
fld3 = Field("Ease of use", [s1], "1 = very hard, 5 = very easy")
s1 = Slider("Ease of use", $ease, 1, 5)
fld4 = Field("Support quality", [s2], "1 = poor, 5 = excellent")
s2 = Slider("Support quality", $support, 1, 5)
fld5 = Field("Comments", [t1])
t1 = Textarea("What should we improve?", $comments, "Tell us what worked and what didn't")
fld6 = Field("Recommendation", [sw1])
sw1 = Switch("I would recommend this product", $recommend)
btn1 = Button("Submit survey", "notes.create", {title: "Survey response"})
c1 = Card("Live summary", [m1, p1])
m1 = Metric("Average rating", avg, "Ease of use and support, out of 5")
avg = ($ease + $support) / 2
p1 = Progress("Completion", done)
done = $name == "" ? 60 : 100
$name = ""
$overall = "Satisfied"
$ease = 4
$support = 4
$comments = ""
$recommend = true
:::

The two sliders both start at 4, so the average starts at 4.0 — move them to see the metric and completion bar react instantly. Pressing **Submit** saves the response as a note; nothing is sent until you confirm.

results.prompt: Add a form with a name and a comment.
results.raw:
Here's a ready-to-use feedback form with bound inputs:

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
$name = ""
$comment = ""
root = Form("Leave a comment", [f1, f2, actions])
f1 = Field("Name", [i1])
i1 = Input("Your name", $name)
f2 = Field("Comment", [t1], "Share anything you'd like — a few sentences is plenty.")
t1 = Textarea("Your comment", $comment)
actions = Row([bClear])
bClear = Button("Clear", @Reset($name))
:::

A couple of notes on how it behaves:

- Both fields are **live-bound** to local state, so typing updates the values immediately — no model round-trip.
- The **Clear** button resets the name field to its default. If you'd like a real "submit" that saves the entry somewhere or sends it on, tell me the destination (a note, a help desk action, or a follow-up prompt) and I'll wire the button to it.

results.prompt: Explain the water cycle.
results.raw:
The water cycle — also called the hydrological cycle — is the continuous movement of water between the ocean, atmosphere, and land. It has no beginning and no end: the same water molecules have been cycling for billions of years, powered by solar energy and held in place by gravity.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([tl1, tbl1])
tl1 = Timeline("The stages of the cycle", [{title:"1. Evaporation", description:"The Sun heats liquid water in oceans, lakes and rivers; molecules gain enough energy to escape as vapour. About 90% of atmospheric water enters this way.", status:"active"},{title:"2. Transpiration", description:"Plants draw water up through their roots and release it as vapour through tiny leaf pores called stomata. Evaporation plus transpiration is often called 'evapotranspiration'.", status:"active"},{title:"3. Condensation", description:"Rising vapour cools with altitude and condenses onto dust, salt and pollen particles, forming tiny droplets that make clouds and fog.", status:"active"},{title:"4. Precipitation", description:"Droplets collide and grow until gravity wins. Water returns as rain, snow, sleet or hail — unevenly, which is why some regions are wet and others are arid.", status:"active"},{title:"5. Infiltration and runoff", description:"Some water soaks into soil and refills aquifers. The rest flows over the surface as runoff, carving streams and rivers that carry it downhill.", status:"active"},{title:"6. Storage and return", description:"Water rests in reservoirs — oceans, ice sheets, lakes, groundwater — until evaporation or flow moves it on again, closing the loop.", status:"active"}])
tbl1 = Table("How long water lingers in each reservoir (average)", ["Reservoir", "Average residence time"], [["Atmosphere", "about 9 days"],["Rivers and streams", "2-6 months"],["Soil moisture", "1-2 months"],["Lakes", "about 50 years"],["Shallow groundwater", "100-200 years"],["Glaciers and ice caps", "about 1,600 years"],["Ocean", "about 3,200 years"],["Deep groundwater", "up to 10,000 years"]])
:::

Two things follow from those numbers. First, the cycle moves enormous volumes of water but very unevenly in time — the ocean is a slow, deep store while the atmosphere is a fast, shallow one, which is why a drought can persist even though the planet holds plenty of water. Second, the cycle is a distillation system: evaporation leaves salts behind, so the vapour that rains down is fresh water. That is the mechanism that keeps supplying the freshwater rivers, lakes and aquifers we depend on — and it is also why groundwater extracted from deep aquifers is effectively a non-renewable resource on human timescales.

Human activity alters the cycle in two main ways: greenhouse gases warm the air so it holds more moisture, making heavy rainfall and drought more intense, while land use — deforestation, paving, irrigation — changes how much water infiltrates versus runs off, which raises flood risk and depletes aquifers.
